misconception_description: Student believes that variable names containing vowels can only store string values, while consonant-only names can store any type.

solutions.generated_code:
program CekTandaBerlawanan
kamus
  x, y : integer
  hasil : boolean
algoritma
  input(x, y)
  x <- integer(x)
  y <- integer(y)
  if (x < 0 and y > 0) or (x > 0 and y < 0) then
    hasil <- true
  else
    hasil <- false
  endif
  output(hasil)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student renamed the parameters from x,y to num1,num2. Since 'num' contains the vowel 'u', the student believes these parameters can only hold string values. Therefore, they immediately convert num1 and num2 to integers using int() and store them in consonant-only variable names (x, y) which they believe can properly hold integer values. The student is confident this is the correct approach - they think the XOR operation requires actual integers, not "string integers", so the conversion is necessary. While this code works correctly (int() on an integer just returns the integer), it reveals the student's misconception about Python's type system and variable naming. The unnecessary conversions don't break the functionality but demonstrate the false belief that vowel-containing variable names impose type restrictions.
